action_criteria.expected_evidence: Polyradiculoneuropathy pattern (demyelinating or axonal features, absent F-waves, sural sparing where present); may be normal in the first week
action_criteria.label: Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Nerve conduction studies at the bedside show the demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy that separates GBS from a brainstem or cord lesion and from critical illness neuropathy; early studies are abnormal in F-waves and distal latencies first [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Baseline values before treatment, with a normal and stable platelet count, normal potassium and reduced eGFR; coagulation and the apixaban level frame the timing of the lumbar puncture; abnormal liver tests or low albumin mark a higher risk of a severe course
action_criteria.label: Baseline blood tests: full blood count, renal function and electrolytes, liver tests, albumin, glucose, CK and coagulation
action_criteria.rationale: Baseline blood tests, including the platelet count and coagulation with an apixaban level before the lumbar puncture in a patient on triple antithrombotic therapy; the platelet count also answers the HIT question after heparin during PCI [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Triple antithrombotic therapy sets the timing of the LP and the safety of a central line for plasma exchange, while the recent stent forbids a lapse in antiplatelet cover; lisinopril matters for albumin exchange; IVIg adds a thrombotic risk after the infarct
action_criteria.label: Check the medication list for interactions with apixaban, aspirin, ticagrelor and lisinopril before LP and IVIg or plasma exchange
action_criteria.rationale: Apixaban, aspirin and ticagrelor change when and whether the LP is done, and lisinopril changes how plasma exchange is given; IVIg carries a thrombotic warning 3 days after a myocardial infarction.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Albuminocytological dissociation: raised protein with cells <5/mm3 (5-50/mm3 compatible but prompts an alternative; >50/mm3 suggests another diagnosis); protein may be normal in the first week
action_criteria.label: Lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein and glucose
action_criteria.rationale: CSF supports the diagnosis and excludes an infective or inflammatory alternative, but here it is not a prerequisite for the assessment: she is on apixaban (anti-Xa in the on-treatment range) with aspirin and ticagrelor that cannot be interrupted after the stent, so the puncture follows the coagulation tests and the medication review and is done only after an agreed interval from the last apixaban dose; the clinical picture and the NCS suffice to start IVIg, which is not delayed for it [EAN_PNS_2023, Brighton_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC in L, % predicted and mL/kg, MIP and MEP, with the trend; ICU-level monitoring if FVC <20 mL/kg or <60% predicted, MIP weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O, a fall of more than 30%, or bulbar weakness with weak cough
action_criteria.label: Bedside respiratory function (FVC, MIP, MEP), repeated serially while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: Her FVC, MIP and MEP before intubation document the respiratory failure and the rate of decline; they set the baseline for weaning and for the treatment decision [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous telemetry with blood pressure monitoring: atrial fibrillation at 52-128 bpm with a longest RR interval of 2.4 s and labile blood pressure 104/58 to 196/108 mmHg in the first 24 hours; autonomic instability (rate and blood pressure lability, bradyarrhythmia) requires continued monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.label: Continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: Autonomic dysfunction is common in severe GBS, and 3 days after a myocardial infarction with atrial fibrillation the arrhythmia risk is higher still; monitoring continues while weakness progresses [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Atrial fibrillation at 104 bpm with inferior Q waves from the recent infarction and a prolonged QTc of 472 ms
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline 12-lead ECG screens for autonomic rhythm and conduction changes and gives the QTc before treatment [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on immunotherapy in GBS; not needed for the diagnosis or the treatment decision
action_criteria.label: Optional literature search on IVIg versus plasma exchange in GBS
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].
Do not start IVIg without checking renal function.
Do not stop dual antiplatelet therapy without cardiology input (stent thrombosis risk after recent PCI).
required_recommendations: Continue mechanical ventilation in the ICU: before intubation her FVC was 1.0 L (16 mL/kg, below 20 mL/kg), MIP -20 cmH2O and MEP 28 cmH2O, falling 38% in 6 hours, with bulbar weakness and a weak cough; avoid succinylcholine for any further airway procedure (denervation hyperkalaemia) [EAN_PNS_2023, Lawn_2001].

Start IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total, about 26 g/day at 64.5 kg) now, at the lowest practical infusion rate with adequate hydration and monitoring of renal function, given the thrombotic warning after a recent infarct; plasma exchange is an equivalent alternative with relative cautions here (triple antithrombotic therapy and central access, haemodynamics after the infarct, lisinopril held for 24 hours before albumin exchange) [EAN_PNS_2023].

Agree the lumbar puncture with cardiology: antiplatelet therapy is not interrupted after the recent stent, so the puncture is done only if the team judges the bleeding risk acceptable, after an agreed interval from the last apixaban dose guided by the anti-Xa level; do not delay IVIg for it.

Continuous cardiac telemetry with arterial blood pressure monitoring in the ICU while weakness progresses: autonomic instability adds to the arrhythmia risk of the recent infarct and atrial fibrillation; review metoprolol against bradyarrhythmia.
Hold metformin while renal function is reduced after contrast and she is critically ill.

avoided_actions.rationale: She is alert and follows commands with no seizure or encephalopathy; EEG has no role in an areflexic polyradiculoneuropathy.
A head CT on day 1 was unremarkable apart from the old infarct; flaccid areflexic weakness with distal sensory loss is a lower motor neuron pattern that a repeat CT does not address.
Functional or metabolic brain imaging adds nothing to a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.

Cerebrovascular imaging is not indicated: weakness spreading from the hands to the legs over a day with areflexia, distal sensory loss, full eye movements, normal facial strength and preserved alertness is not a brainstem stroke.

accepted: Severe Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) after myocardial infarction and PCI

differential.key_features: Heparin was given during PCI, but the platelet count is 236 x10^9/L with no fall, onset was 20 hours after exposure rather than 5-10 days, and the weakness is symmetric, flaccid and areflexic rather than focal and thrombotic.
Onset 20 hours after the infarct, before the 1-2 weeks of critical illness these need, with no sepsis or multiorgan failure, raised CSF protein and a demyelinating NCS.

Atrial fibrillation and a recent infarct raise it, but weakness spread from the hands to the legs over a day with areflexia, distal sensory loss, full eye movements, normal facial strength and preserved alertness, and the day 1 CT showed no acute lesion.

differential.diagnosis: Spinal epidural haematoma or spinal cord infarction
differential.key_features: Triple antithrombotic therapy and angiography raise them, but bulbar weakness places the process above the cord, there is no back pain, sensory level or early sphincter involvement, and the NCS shows a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.
Procalcitonin 1.69 and CRP 28.4 after the infarct and PCI, but she is afebrile with a normal white count, chest clear, urine clear and an acellular CSF with negative Gram stain and culture.
Symmetric weakness over hours with no multifocal pattern, rash or systemic features.
Cannot be excluded at presentation; progression beyond 8 weeks or 3 or more treatment-related fluctuations would point to it. Reassess at 8 weeks.

key_clinical_evidence: Flaccid areflexic quadriparesis with bulbar weakness progressing over a day with a demyelinating NCS meets Brighton level 2 without the CSF; raised CSF protein with 3 cells/mm3, once the puncture is judged safe, makes it level 1 when the course plateaus within 4 weeks [Brighton_2011].
Onset 20 hours after the infarct and PCI is far shorter than the usual interval after an antecedent event; the diagnosis rests on the clinical, CSF and NCS findings, not on a trigger.
Critical illness polyneuropathy and myopathy need 1-2 weeks of critical illness; weakness 20 hours after an infarct with a demyelinating NCS is not CIP.
A normal, stable platelet count makes HIT very unlikely, and procalcitonin and CRP rise after myocardial infarction and PCI without infection.
Anti-ganglioside antibodies are not needed to diagnose typical GBS; anti-GQ1b is tested when Miller Fisher syndrome or an overlap is suspected [EAN_PNS_2023].

Apixaban, aspirin and ticagrelor shape the timing of the lumbar puncture and the choice between IVIg and plasma exchange; dual antiplatelet therapy is not stopped after a recent stent without cardiology.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The symmetric lower motor neuron pattern with bulbar weakness, raised CSF protein and a demyelinating NCS is a polyradiculoneuropathy; the timing is coincidental or too short to be a usual trigger.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute myocardial infarction treated with PCI 20 hours before the weakness began
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors on a cardioembolic or procedural complication (stroke, cord infarction) or treats the infarct as the cause of GBS.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Raised procalcitonin and CRP after MI and PCI: post-procedural inflammation; no infective focus; CSF acellular.
red_herrings.data_point: Raised procalcitonin (1.69 ng/mL) and CRP (28.4 mg/L)

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The platelet count is normal with no fall, onset was 20 hours after exposure, and the deficit is symmetric and areflexic rather than focal.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with a thrombotic neurological complication.

sequence_constraints.reason: The platelet count, coagulation and apixaban level are checked before a lumbar puncture in a patient on apixaban, aspirin and ticagrelor.
The antithrombotic medicines are reviewed before the lumbar puncture: apixaban needs an interval after the last dose, and dual antiplatelet therapy must not be stopped after a recent stent.
Renal function and the blood count are reviewed with the medication list before IVIg or plasma exchange is chosen.

interactions: Apixaban with aspirin and ticagrelor (triple antithrombotic therapy): additive bleeding risk. Neuraxial puncture during anticoagulation carries a risk of spinal epidural haematoma; labelling and regional anaesthesia guidance give drug-specific intervals after the last dose (relative caution, product labelling).
Ticagrelor and aspirin after a recent coronary stent: premature interruption of dual antiplatelet therapy raises the risk of stent thrombosis (product labelling warning).
Antithrombotic therapy and plasma exchange: central venous catheter placement and the exchange itself add bleeding risk (relative caution).

Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) and albumin-replacement plasma exchange: bradykinin-mediated flushing, hypotension and bradycardia during apheresis; the ACE inhibitor is usually held for at least 24 hours before an exchange (category-level caution).
IVIg: thromboembolic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke, are reported, with higher risk in older patients, known vascular disease and hyperviscosity (product labelling boxed warning).
IVIg and renal function: renal dysfunction is reported, more often with sucrose-stabilised products (relative caution with reduced eGFR).
Metformin: reduced renal function and recent iodinated contrast increase the risk of lactic acidosis (product labelling).
Metoprolol: additive negative chronotropic effect with autonomic bradyarrhythmia (relative caution).
general.proposed: Lumbar puncture, IVIg or plasma exchange; current medicines apixaban, aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, atorvastatin, lisinopril, metformin
general.summary: Category-level cautions: three antithrombotic drugs bear on neuraxial puncture and line placement, dual antiplatelet therapy must not lapse after a recent stent, an ACE inhibitor reacts with albumin-replacement apheresis, and IVIg carries thrombotic and renal warnings.
warnings: No interaction identified between IVIg or plasma exchange and atorvastatin.

results.finding: Guidelines for adults with GBS who cannot walk unaided advise IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days within 2 weeks of onset or plasma exchange within 4 weeks, with no preference between them; corticosteroids are not advised.
A second IVIg course in patients with a poor predicted prognosis did not improve outcome and caused more serious adverse events.

general.summary: IVIg or plasma exchange is advised for adults with GBS unable to walk unaided; neither is preferred, and a second IVIg course is not advised [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL study (bedside, cardiac ICU day 3). 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in median, ulnar and peroneal motor nerves, with conduction block in the ulnar forearm segment. 2. Reduced CMAP amplitudes, which this early may reflect distal conduction block as well as axonal loss. 3. Absent F-waves and H-reflexes. 4. Absent median and sural sensory responses; a pre-existing diabetic neuropathy cannot be separated on this study. 5. Reduced recruitment without denervation on needle EMG. Findings are consistent with an acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

metadata.difficulty_description: Severe GBS 20 hours after MI and PCI in a patient on apixaban, aspirin and ticagrelor: stroke, cord haematoma, HIT, sepsis and critical illness neuropathy must be separated, and the LP and treatment planned around triple antithrombotic therapy.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required actions (NCS/EMG, baseline labs with coagulation, interaction check, respiratory function, telemetry) and a recommended CSF that must follow the labs and the interaction check and waits for a safe interval after apixaban; 3 red herrings (MI/PCI timing, procalcitonin and CRP, heparin exposure).
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 GBS audit: spine MRI is optional and limited to five cases with a concrete cord, traumatic, postoperative or infiltrative alternative; generic hidden MRI reports removed.

patient.chief_complaint: Weakness spreading from the hands to all four limbs, with bulbar weakness, beginning about 20 hours after emergency PCI for acute myocardial infarction; intubated in the cardiac ICU.

family_history: Hypertension in family; no neurological disease
past_medical_history: Remote ischaemic stroke, no residual deficits
Acute inferior-posterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction 3 days ago, treated with PCI to the mid RCA (see history of present illness)

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Z. is a 73-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation on apixaban and a remote ischaemic stroke without residual deficits. Three days ago (cardiac ICU day 0) she presented with an acute inferior-posterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction with right ventricular involvement. Emergency angiography showed a 90% proximal LAD stenosis, an occluded distal posterolateral branch and an 85% mid RCA stenosis with thrombus; she had PCI to the mid RCA through the right radial artery with unfractionated heparin, and was started on aspirin and ticagrelor alongside her apixaban. Peak troponin I was 14.6 ng/mL. About 20 hours after the PCI (day 1) she reported numbness and weakness of both hands, spreading to the forearms and then the legs over the following hours. A head CT on day 1 was unremarkable apart from the old infarct. By day 2 she could not lift her arms or legs, her speech was slurred, her cough was weak and her SpO2 fell to 93% on 4 L of oxygen; she was intubated in the cardiac ICU on day 2. Her son reports no diarrhoea, respiratory infection or fever in the previous 6 weeks and no new medicine apart from those started after the PCI. She has no bladder or bowel symptoms before catheterisation and no back or neck pain. Sedation was paused for the neurological assessment today (day 3).

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Day 3 (intubated): pupils equal and reactive; eye movements full, no ptosis; facial strength normal bilaterally; gag reduced bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Not tested (intubated, unable to move the legs against gravity).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Day 3, sedation paused: alert and anxious; follows commands and answers yes/no questions by head nod.
neurological_exam.motor: Day 3: flaccid weakness of all four limbs. Shoulder abduction 2/5, elbow flexion 2/5, wrist extension 1/5, hip flexion 1/5, knee extension 1/5, ankle dorsiflexion 0/5 bilaterally (MRC sum score 14/60). Neck flexion 2/5.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent throughout (biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, knee and ankle) bilaterally. Plantar responses mute.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced pinprick in a glove-and-stocking distribution to the wrists and mid-shins; vibration absent at the toes and reduced at the ankles. No sensory level on the trunk.

physical_exam.general: Weight 64.5 kg, height 158 cm. Intubated and ventilated. Right radial access site clean, without haematoma. Chest clear on auscultation; no peripheral oedema. Urinary catheter in place, urine clear. No rash or joint swelling.
